title: Bangladesh Measles Death Toll Reaches 780 as Vaccine Gaps Persist
excerpt: One more child died with measles-like symptoms in the latest 24-hour reporting period, as the outbreak that began in early 2026 continues to claim young lives despite an emergency vaccination campaign reaching millions.
body:
• Bangladesh's combined confirmed and suspected measles death toll has reached 780, with one more child dying in the 24 hours to 17 July, according to the DGHS.
  • Over 116,000 suspected cases and more than 14,200 confirmed infections have been recorded since the outbreak began in early 2026.
  • Vaccine procurement failures following the 2024 political upheaval left millions of children unprotected, fuelling the worst measles crisis in Bangladesh's recent history.
  • An emergency vaccination campaign has reached nearly 18 million children, but experts warn the outbreak is far from over.

One More Death as Toll Climbs

One more child died with measles-like symptoms in the 24-hour period ending 8 am on 17 July, bringing Bangladesh's combined tally of confirmed and suspected measles-related deaths to 780, the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) reported on Thursday.

Of the total fatalities, 685 are classified as suspected measles deaths while 95 have been laboratory-confirmed, the DGHS said. During the same reporting period, 873 new suspected cases were recorded, pushing the nationwide cumulative total past 116,000. Laboratory-confirmed infections rose by 140 to reach 14,244.

The day before, the toll had risen sharply — eight children died in a single 24-hour window, raising the count from 771 to 779 on 16 July. That daily fluctuation underscores a pattern health officials have tracked for months: while the pace of new infections appears to be easing compared to peaks in April and May, children continue to die at an alarming rate.

Roots of the Crisis

The epidemic, which began in Rohingya refugee camps near the Myanmar border in January 2026, has now engulfed nearly all of Bangladesh's 64 districts. Its roots trace to a breakdown in vaccine procurement following the country's 2024 political upheaval, when the interim government switched from UNICEF-managed procurement to an open-tender system.

""At this rate of vaccination, the infection will not decrease right now," he said."

That transition triggered bureaucratic delays and nationwide vaccine stockouts. A supplemental measles-rubella immunisation campaign, originally planned for 2024 and postponed due to political unrest, was ultimately cancelled. By late March 2026, government data indicated only 59 percent of eligible children had received their measles vaccination in 2025 — far below the 95 percent threshold needed to prevent outbreaks.

"Beyond immunization gaps, Bangladesh's measles crisis reflects deep structural weaknesses."

— Mohammad Mushtuq Husain, Adviser, Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research (IEDCR)

Malnutrition has compounded the toll. Roughly 28 percent of Bangladeshi children under five are stunted and 10 percent suffer from wasting, according to Science magazine. Vitamin A deficiency, worsened after three missed biannual distribution campaigns since 2024, further weakens children's immune defences. Overcrowded, underfunded hospitals have struggled to cope, with some facilities in Dhaka treating children on floors when beds ran out.

Emergency Campaign and Its Limits

The government, working with UNICEF, WHO, and Gavi, launched an emergency measles-rubella vaccination campaign in April 2026, initially targeting children aged six months to five years in 18 high-risk districts before expanding nationwide. By mid-May, nearly 18 million children had received at least one dose, according to government data cited by Save the Children.

Nine out of ten cases have occurred in children aged one to 14, the WHO has reported, with roughly three-quarters of infections in under-fives. In Cox's Bazar, home to about one million Rohingya refugees, three-quarters of laboratory-confirmed cases were in children who were either unvaccinated or only partially vaccinated.

"Measles is almost entirely preventable and it is devastating that so many children have lost their lives because of a lack of vaccines."

— Shumon Sengupta, Country Director, Save the Children Bangladesh

Since the DGHS began issuing daily updates on 15 March, a total of 98,600 patients with suspected measles have been hospitalised. Of those, 95,031 have recovered and been discharged — a recovery rate that offers some reassurance, but one that masks the ongoing risk to malnourished and unvaccinated children.

A Diaspora Watching With Alarm

For the large Bangladeshi diaspora, the crisis has been a source of deep anxiety. Families abroad have been sending money for treatment and pressing relatives to vaccinate children. The WHO has also warned of a "considerable risk" of the outbreak spreading to neighbouring Myanmar and India, where immunisation has also been disrupted — a concern shared by South Asian communities worldwide.

What Comes Next

The newly elected government of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman reinstated vaccine procurement through UNICEF in April and has pledged to resume Vitamin A distribution. But experts caution the campaign will take time to close immunity gaps across a population of over 175 million.

Former disease control director Be-nazir Ahmed has warned that the current pace of vaccination is insufficient to quickly curb transmission. "At this rate of vaccination, the infection will not decrease right now," he said. With over 800 new suspected cases still being reported daily, the crisis that turned a preventable childhood illness into Bangladesh's deadliest outbreak in recent memory is not over.
